etymology: The inordinate exaltation of self; from the Old English pryde, haughtiness; the root sin of the fallen heart.
biblical_def: Pride is the inordinate exaltation of self—the lifting up of the heart against God and above one’s fellow men—and Scripture treats it as the root and mother of sin. It was pride that cast down the anointed cherub, who said in his heart, I will be like the most High; pride that the serpent stirred in Eve with the promise, ye shall be as gods; pride that is the first of the things the LORD hates, a proud look heading the list of seven abominations. The fear of the LORD is to hate evil, and chiefly pride, arrogancy, and the froward mouth, which God hates. Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall; the pride of life is not of the Father but of the world. Above all, pride sets a man against the grace of God, for God resists the proud but gives grace unto the humble—the proud heart will not stoop to receive salvation as a free gift, insisting on its own worth and its own way. The dictionary reads pride as the original and besetting sin, the self set up where God should be, the spring of unbelief, rebellion, and contempt of others; and it answers pride with the humility that the gospel both requires and works—the bowing of the self before God, who gives His grace to the lowly and brings down everyone that is proud and lifted up.
webster_summary: The inordinate exaltation of self against God and above men; the root sin of the fallen heart, which God resists, answered by the humility the gospel works.
webster_full: PRIDE, the inordinate exaltation of self against God and above men.
The root and mother of sin, from the fall of the cherub to the fall of Eve.
Pride goeth before destruction, an haughty spirit before a fall (Pro 16:18).
The pride of life is not of the Father but of the world (1Jo 2:16).
God resisteth the proud but giveth grace to the humble (Jas 4:6).

Jas 4:6

The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
corruption_summary: The age makes pride a virtue—self-esteem, self-assertion, self-celebration—and renames humility as weakness; Scripture names pride the root sin that God resists and humility the grace He gives.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the modern celebration of pride as a virtue. The age exalts self-esteem, self-assertion, and self-love as the keys to flourishing, and rebrands the very pride Scripture calls the root sin as confidence and authenticity, while sneering at humility as weakness or self-hatred. Whole movements parade the word “pride” as a banner. But God’s verdict does not change: a proud look is the first of the things He hates, pride goes before destruction, and God resists the proud. To call the chief of sins a virtue is to bless the very thing that ruins the soul and bars it from grace.

The principle to recover is the sinfulness of pride and the grace of humility. Pride is the self set up where God should be—the spring of unbelief that will not receive salvation as a gift, of rebellion that will not submit, of contempt that despises others. It must be put to death. God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble; the gospel both requires humility and works it, bowing the sinner to receive Christ and clothing the saint with lowliness. The way up is down: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted, and the lowly find the grace the proud forfeit.
roots_summary: The inordinate exaltation of self against God and above men; the root sin God resists, answered by the humility the gospel works.

etymology: Distressing care and worry over the uncertain future; from the Latin anxietas, from angere, to choke or distress.
biblical_def: Anxiety is the distressing care and worry that chokes the soul with dread over the uncertain future, and Scripture meets it not with scorn but with the tender command to cast our care upon a Father who cares. The dictionary speaks gently here, for the children of God are not promised a life free of fear, and many a faithful saint has wrestled with a heavy and fearful heart; the burdens of body and circumstance are real, and a brother bowed down with anxious dread is to be borne with compassion, not crushed with rebuke. Yet the Word does call the believer away from anxious care and toward trust: be careful for nothing, but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God; cast all your care upon Him, for He careth for you. The Lord bids us take no anxious thought for the morrow, for the heavenly Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies will not fail His children; sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and He shall sustain thee. The dictionary reads anxiety as the choking care that springs, at root, from looking to the uncertain future without looking to the certain God; and it answers anxiety not with the world’s techniques of self-soothing but with the casting of every care, in believing prayer, upon the faithful Father who numbers the hairs of our head and has promised never to leave nor forsake His own.
webster_summary: The distressing care that chokes the soul with dread of the future; met with compassion and answered by casting every care, in believing prayer, upon the Father who cares for His own.
webster_full: ANXIETY, the distressing care and worry over the uncertain future.
Met not with scorn but with the command to cast our care on a caring Father.
Be careful for nothing, but make requests known in prayer (Php 4:6).
Casting all your care upon Him, for He careth for you (1Pe 5:7).
Answered by trust in the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
corruption_summary: The therapy age treats anxiety only as a disorder to be managed by technique, severed from the soul’s relation to God; Scripture meets it with compassion and the casting of every care upon the caring Father.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the therapy culture’s reduction of anxiety to a mere disorder to be managed by technique—breathing, mindfulness, self-talk, and medication alone—severed entirely from the soul’s relation to God and from the sin of unbelief that often lies beneath anxious care. The dictionary does not deny the reality of bodily affliction, nor that some anxiety has physical roots that may warrant lawful means of help; the saint is to be borne with, not browbeaten. But it refuses the framing that treats man as a machine to be soothed and never as a soul made to trust his Maker. Where the world offers only self-management, it leaves the heart still looking to the uncertain future without looking to the certain God.

The principle to recover is the casting of care upon the caring Father. Scripture meets the anxious not with the world’s self-soothing but with a Person: be careful for nothing, but in everything by prayer let your requests be made known; cast all your care upon Him, for He careth for you. Anxious care at root is care that has not yet been cast upon God—the burden carried alone that was meant to be rolled upon the LORD, who sustains and never suffers the righteous to be moved. The Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, who numbers the hairs of our head, bids His fearful children trust Him for the morrow and rest in His unfailing care.
roots_summary: The distressing care that chokes the soul with dread of the future; met with compassion and answered by casting every care upon the caring Father in prayer.

etymology: The state of true blessedness and well-being; from hap, fortune, but raised in Scripture to the settled blessedness of those whose God is the LORD.
biblical_def: Happiness, in the biblical sense, is not the fleeting pleasure the world chases but the settled blessedness of those who are rightly related to God—a deep well-being grounded not in circumstance but in the favor and fellowship of the LORD. Scripture pronounces happy a particular people: happy is that people whose God is the LORD; blessed, or happy, is the man that walks not in the counsel of the ungodly but delights in the law of the LORD; happy is the man that finds wisdom; and the Lord Jesus said, if ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them. This biblical happiness differs from the world’s in its root and its permanence. The world seeks happiness in pleasure, possessions, and self—a happiness that depends on fortune and fails when fortune fails. The Scripture grounds happiness in God Himself: the blessed man is happy because his God is the LORD, his sins forgiven, his delight in the Word, his hope in heaven. Such happiness can stand in poverty and persecution, for the Beatitudes pronounce blessed the poor in spirit, the mourners, the persecuted. The dictionary reads happiness as true blessedness found in God: not the world’s mood that rises and falls with circumstance, but the abiding joy of those whose God is the LORD, who alone is the fountain of pleasures for evermore.
webster_summary: True blessedness grounded in a right relation to God; not the world’s fleeting pleasure but the settled well-being of those whose God is the LORD.
webster_full: HAPPINESS, the settled blessedness of those rightly related to God.
Not the world’s fleeting pleasure but a well-being grounded in the LORD.
Happy is that people whose God is the LORD (Psa 144:15).
Blessed is the man who delights in the law of the LORD (Psa 1:1).
Happy are ye if ye do the things you know (Joh 13:17).

corruption_summary: The world makes happiness a fleeting mood dependent on pleasure and circumstance, pursued as the chief end of man; Scripture grounds true happiness in God, whose favor abides through every loss.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the world’s counterfeit of happiness—a fleeting mood of pleasure and ease, dependent on fortune and circumstance, pursued as the very chief end of man. The age makes “your own happiness” the highest good and the justifier of every choice, even the breaking of vows and the casting off of duty; and the happiness it pursues, being rooted in pleasure and self, fails the moment pleasure fails. This is happiness built on sand. It cannot survive loss, and it leaves the soul, in the end, emptier than before, having sought in the gifts what is found only in the Giver.

The principle to recover is true happiness grounded in God. The blessed man of Scripture is happy not because his circumstances are easy but because his God is the LORD—his sins forgiven, his delight in the Word, his hope laid up in heaven. Such happiness can stand in poverty and persecution, for the Lord pronounces blessed the poor in spirit and the mourners; it does not rise and fall with fortune because its root is in the unchanging God. The chief end of man is not his own happiness but to glorify God and enjoy Him for ever—and in that enjoyment of God is found the only happiness that lasts, fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore.
roots_summary: True blessedness grounded in a right relation to God; not the world’s fleeting pleasure but the settled well-being of those whose God is the LORD.

etymology: The two opposite errors that flank the gospel of grace: legalism (works added to grace) and license (grace abused for sin).
biblical_def: Legalism and license are the two ditches that flank the narrow road of gospel grace, and the believer must be kept from both. Legalism is the error that adds the works of man to the grace of God—making acceptance with God depend, in whole or part, on the keeping of the law or the traditions of men, and binding the conscience with rules God has not commanded. It is the error of the Galatian Judaizers, against whom Paul thundered; it has a show of wisdom in will-worship and the neglecting of the body, but it overthrows justification by faith alone and entangles the freed soul again with the yoke of bondage. License, on the other side, is the abuse of grace as a cloak for sin—the antinomian error that reasons, since we are not under law but under grace, we may sin freely. Paul crushes it: shall we sin because we are under grace? God forbid. He warns the called to liberty not to use their liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love to serve one another. The dictionary reads legalism and license as opposite distortions of the one gospel: the one adds law to grace and so denies grace; the other subtracts holiness from grace and so denies its power. The narrow way between is evangelical liberty—freed from the law as a covenant of works, yet taught by grace to deny ungodliness and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
webster_summary: The two opposite errors flanking gospel grace—legalism, which adds works to grace, and license, which abuses grace for sin; the narrow way between is evangelical liberty.
webster_full: LEGALISM VS. LICENSE, the two ditches that flank gospel grace.
Legalism adds the works of man to the grace of God, binding the conscience.
License abuses grace as a cloak for sin—the antinomian error.
Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ made us free (Gal 5:1).
Grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and live soberly and godly (Tit 2:12).

Gal 5:13

corruption_summary: Both ditches corrupt the gospel: legalism adds law to grace and denies grace; license subtracts holiness from grace and denies its power; the narrow way is evangelical liberty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The two corruptions are perennial and opposite. Legalism adds the works of man to the grace of God—whether by the Judaizer’s law-keeping, the ritualist’s ceremonies, or the modern moralist’s rules—and so makes acceptance turn on human performance, denying justification by faith alone and entangling the conscience with a yoke of bondage. License runs the other way, abusing the freeness of grace as a license to sin, reasoning that grace covers all so holiness may be neglected—the antinomian error Paul answers with God forbid. The one is religion without grace; the other is grace without godliness; both miss the gospel.

The principle to recover is evangelical liberty, the narrow road between the ditches. Christ has made the believer free—free from the law as a covenant of works and from the bondage of man’s traditions—and the soul is to stand fast in that liberty against the legalist. Yet liberty is not license: it is not to be used for an occasion to the flesh but as freedom to serve in love. The same grace that justifies apart from works also teaches us to deny ungodliness and to live soberly, righteously, and godly. Grace neither adds law to itself nor excuses sin; it frees and it sanctifies.

etymology: A solemn, voluntary promise made to God; from the Latin votum, a thing solemnly promised.
biblical_def: A vow is a solemn, voluntary promise made to God, binding the one who makes it to perform what he has promised. Scripture treats vows with great seriousness. They are not required—a man is free not to vow—but once made, they must be paid: when thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it, for He hath no pleasure in fools; pay that which thou hast vowed. Indeed, better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay; for the LORD thy God will surely require it, and it would be sin to slack. The Scripture both warns against rash vowing—letting the mouth run ahead of the heart and binding oneself to what one will not perform—and commends the godly vow rightly made and faithfully kept: vow, and pay unto the LORD your God. Vows ought to be made only to God, of things lawful and within one’s power, in faith and conscience of duty, and once made are to be performed though it cost. The dictionary reads the vow as a sacred and binding word given to God, to be entered soberly and kept faithfully: not multiplied rashly nor made of unlawful things, but, when lawfully made, paid without delay—for God is in heaven and we upon earth, and He who hears our words will require them at our hand.
webster_summary: A solemn, voluntary promise made to God; not required, but once made to be paid faithfully—better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age of broken promises makes vows light—in marriage, church membership, and word; Scripture binds the lawful vow as a sacred debt to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the cheapening of the vow in an age of broken promises. Marriage vows—made before God for life—are abandoned at the first hardness; church covenants are entered lightly and forsaken; the very weight of a solemn word given to God is forgotten, so that men vow rashly and break freely. But Scripture will not have it so. A vow is a sacred debt: defer not to pay it; the LORD will surely require it; it would be sin to slack. To break a lawful vow is not a small thing but a lie before the God who heard it and who has no pleasure in fools.

The principle to recover is the sober making and faithful keeping of vows. The Scripture neither forbids vows nor multiplies them: a man is free not to vow, and better not to vow than to vow and not pay; rash vowing, letting the mouth outrun the heart, is folly. But the lawful vow—made to God alone, of things lawful and within one’s power, in faith and conscience of duty—binds the conscience and must be performed, though it cost. The believer weighs his vows before he makes them and keeps them after, remembering that God is in heaven and will require the words of our lips.

etymology: A solemn calling of God to witness the truth of what one affirms or promises; from the Old English āth.
biblical_def: An oath is a solemn calling of God to witness the truth of what one affirms or the sincerity of what one promises, invoking Him as the judge of one’s words. The dictionary follows the Reformed and confessional understanding, which distinguishes the lawful oath from vain and profane swearing. A lawful oath is a part of religious worship, in which the one swearing solemnly appeals to God to witness the truth and to judge him according to the truth or falsehood of what he swears; God Himself commanded, thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and shalt swear by His name, and an oath for confirmation is to men an end of all strife. God Himself confirmed His promise to Abraham with an oath. But the Lord Jesus, when He said, Swear not at all, and James, when he said, swear not, neither by heaven nor by the earth, but let your yea be yea, forbade the rash, casual, and profane swearing by which men in that day laced their common speech with light oaths—not the solemn judicial oath rightly taken before God or magistrate. The dictionary reads the oath as a lawful and weighty act of worship when made of things true and right, in the name of God alone, with reverence; and it condemns the vain swearing—the careless oath, the profane use of God’s name, the false oath—that takes the holy name in vain, which the LORD will not hold guiltless.
webster_summary: A solemn calling of God to witness the truth of one’s word; lawful and an act of worship when rightly made, but vain and profane swearing is forbidden and takes God’s name in vain.
webster_full: OATH, a solemn calling of God to witness the truth of one’s word.

corruption_summary: Some misread “swear not at all” to forbid every oath, including lawful ones; the confessional reading distinguishes the lawful judicial oath, an act of worship, from the vain and profane swearing Christ condemned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the right reading of the Lord’s “swear not at all.” Some (the Anabaptists and others) take it to forbid every oath whatsoever, even the lawful oath before a magistrate; but this sets the Lord against the law that commanded swearing by God’s name, against His own confirming of His promise to Abraham by an oath, and against the apostle Paul, who himself called God to witness. The confessional reading, which the dictionary follows, understands the Lord and James to forbid the rash, casual, and profane swearing that filled common speech—the light oaths by heaven and earth, the careless invoking of the holy name—not the solemn judicial oath rightly taken.

The principle to recover is the lawful oath as an act of worship and the gravity of God’s name. A lawful oath, made of things true and just, in the name of God alone, with reverence and in conscience of duty, is good and an end of strife. But the third commandment stands: the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh His name in vain. The careless oath, the profane curse, the false swearing that calls God to witness a lie—these are grave sins against the holy name. The believer’s speech is to be so truthful that his yea is yea and his nay nay, and his rare lawful oath taken with the fear of God.

etymology: The testing of faith by affliction, by which it is proved and refined; from the Latin triare, to sift or test.
biblical_def: The trial of faith is the testing of the believer’s faith by affliction, temptation, and hardship—the fire by which God proves its genuineness and refines it to greater purity. Scripture teaches the saint to read his trials this way and even to rejoice in them: count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations, knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. Peter calls the trial of faith more precious than gold that perishes, though it be tried with fire, that it might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. The afflictions of the believer are not the wrath of a judge but the refining of a Father, who chastens those He loves and purges the gold of true faith from the dross. Job, in the furnace, confessed the hope of every tried saint: when He hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold. The trial does not destroy true faith but proves and strengthens it, as the storm roots the tree; counterfeit faith withers in the fire, but genuine faith is found at the last unto praise and glory. The dictionary reads the trial of faith as the appointed school of the Christian life—the Father’s refining fire, hard to the flesh but precious to the soul—by which faith is proved real, patience is wrought, the believer is conformed to Christ, and gold is brought forth from the furnace to the praise of God.
webster_summary: The testing of faith by affliction, by which God proves and refines it; more precious than gold tried in the fire, working patience and bringing forth gold to the praise of God.

corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel promises the faithful exemption from trial, and the age reads all suffering as meaningless; Scripture reads the trial of faith as the Father’s refining fire that proves and purifies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors press against the doctrine. The first is the prosperity gospel, which promises the faithful exemption from trial and reads affliction as a sign of too little faith—the very opposite of Scripture, which counts the trial of faith precious and appoints it for the truest saints. The second is the secular reading of suffering as sheer meaningless misfortune, with no Father behind it and no purpose in it, leaving the sufferer only to endure or escape. Both miss the biblical truth that the believer’s trials are neither a sign of God’s absence nor a random cruelty, but the wise appointment of a refining Father.

The principle to recover is the trial of faith as the Father’s refining fire. Affliction is the furnace in which God proves the genuineness of faith and purges its dross, working patience and conforming the believer to Christ. The saint is therefore to count it all joy—not because the fire is pleasant but because its end is precious: a faith found, at the appearing of Jesus Christ, unto praise and honour and glory. Job in his furnace held the hope of all the tried: when He hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold. The God who chastens does so in love, and the gold He brings forth is to His own praise and the believer’s everlasting good.

etymology: The shortness of human life; from the Latin brevitas, shortness; the biblical theme of man’s fleeting days.
biblical_def: The brevity of life is the constant biblical theme of the shortness of man’s days—a vapor, a shadow, a handbreadth—set over against the eternity of God, and pressed upon the soul to teach it wisdom. What is your life? asks James; it is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. The psalmist measures the span: the days of our years are threescore years and ten, and if by strength fourscore, yet is their strength labour and sorrow, for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. He prays to know his end and the measure of his days, that he may know how frail he is. This is no morbid brooding but the path to wisdom: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. To reckon life short is to weigh rightly the things of time and eternity—to loosen the grip on the perishing, to redeem the fleeting hours, to set the affections on the world that does not pass away, and to make ready to meet God. The dictionary reads the brevity of life as a sober and salutary truth: man’s days are few and swift, a vapor soon gone, and the wise man, instead of living as though life were long, numbers his short days, lays up treasure in heaven, and prepares his soul for the eternity that follows the handbreadth of his years.
webster_summary: The shortness of human life—a vapor, a shadow, a handbreadth—set against the eternity of God, pressed upon the soul to teach it to number its days unto wisdom.

corruption_summary: The age hides death and dreams of indefinitely extended life, refusing to number its days; Scripture presses the brevity of life upon the soul to teach it wisdom and to make it ready for eternity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the modern flight from the brevity of life. The age hides death behind hospital walls, fills the days with distraction, and dreams of indefinitely extending the span by medicine and technology, refusing to reckon that man’s days are a vapor soon gone. So men live as though life were long—hoarding, postponing, neglecting the soul—and are overtaken unready, like the rich fool whose barns were full the night his soul was required. To refuse to number one’s days is not to lengthen them but to waste them.

The principle to recover is the numbering of our short days unto wisdom. Scripture presses the brevity of life not to drive the soul to despair but to wake it to wisdom: what is your life? a vapor; our days are threescore and ten, soon cut off; so teach us to number them. The man who reckons his life a handbreadth holds the perishing loosely, redeems the fleeting time, sets his affection on the eternal world, and makes ready to meet his God. The shortness of life, rightly weighed, is a mercy that turns the heart from the dust to the things that abide for ever.

etymology: The leading of God’s people in the way they should go, by His Word, providence, and Spirit; from the Latin divinus and the Old French guider, to lead.
biblical_def: Divine guidance is the gracious leading of God’s people in the way they should go—His direction of their steps by His Word, His providence, and His Spirit. Scripture is full of the promise: in all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths; I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go, I will guide thee with mine eye; thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it. The chief and sufficient means of guidance is the written Word—thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path—which makes plain the will of God in all things needful for faith and life. Where Scripture has not spoken to the particulars of a decision, God guides His people by sanctified wisdom drawn from the Word, by godly counsel, by the ordering of providence, and by the inward working of the Spirit conforming the heart to His will—never by new revelation added to the closed canon. The dictionary reads divine guidance as the believer’s confidence that the God who orders all things will lead His trusting child: not by voices and signs sought apart from Scripture, but by His Word as the lamp, His providence as the path, and His Spirit applying the Word—so that the man who acknowledges God in all his ways and leans not on his own understanding shall find his steps directed by a faithful and all-wise Guide.

corruption_summary: Guidance is sought through subjective impressions, signs, and “words from the Lord” set beside or above Scripture; true guidance comes chiefly by the sufficient Word, with wisdom, counsel, and providence under it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the seeking of divine guidance through subjective impressions, signs, fleeces, and private “words from the Lord” set beside or above the Scripture. Much popular Christianity teaches believers to await an inner voice or mystical nudge for every decision, treating hunches as revelation and so opening the door to self-deception and to a guidance that bypasses the Word. But God does not lead His people by new revelations added to the closed canon; the man who governs his steps by impressions has no sure rule and is tossed by his own feelings dressed up as the Spirit’s voice.

The principle to recover is guidance chiefly by the sufficient Word. The Scripture is the lamp to the feet and the light to the path, making plain the will of God in all that is needful; where it has spoken, the believer obeys, and where it has not spoken to the particulars, God guides by sanctified wisdom drawn from the Word, by godly counsel, by the ordering of providence, and by the Spirit conforming the heart to His revealed will. The believer who acknowledges God in all his ways and leans not on his own understanding is promised a directed path—not by voices sought apart from Scripture, but by the faithful God who leads His trusting child through His Word and His providence.

etymology: The state of being prepared and watchful; from the Old English ræde, ready, prepared; the posture of the watching servant.
biblical_def: Readiness is the settled state of being prepared and watchful for the coming of the Lord and for the meeting with God—the posture of the servant who keeps his loins girded and his lamp burning, looking for his master’s return. The Lord pressed it again and again: be ye also ready, for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh; let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning, like men that wait for their lord. The day of the Lord comes as a thief in the night, at an hour unknown, and only the ready will not be ashamed at His coming. The prophet’s word to a careless nation is the word to every soul: prepare to meet thy God. Readiness is not a frantic last-minute scramble but the steady, watchful, obedient life of one who lives each day as though it might be his last and the Lord’s return near—keeping accounts short with God, his lamp trimmed with the oil of grace, his work faithfully done, his heart set on his Master. The dictionary reads readiness as the watchful preparedness of the believer for death and for the coming of Christ: the wise virgin’s oil in the lamp, the faithful servant found at his post, the soul prepared to meet its God—for the Son of man comes at an hour when men think not, and blessed is that servant whom his Lord, when He cometh, shall find watching.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age lives as though death and judgment will never come; Scripture commands the watchful readiness of the servant who waits for his Master.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the practical unreadiness of an age that lives as though death and judgment will never come. Men put far off the day of reckoning, fill their barns and their schedules, and never make ready to meet their God, as though the Son of man would not come and the soul would not be required. But the Lord’s warning stands: He comes at an hour when men think not, as a thief in the night, and the unready will be overtaken and ashamed. To live unprepared for death and the coming of Christ is the great folly, however full the barns.

The principle to recover is watchful readiness as the posture of the Christian life. The Lord bids His servants keep their loins girded and their lamps burning, waiting for their Master’s return; the wise virgin has oil in her lamp, the faithful servant is found at his post. Readiness is not a frantic deathbed scramble but the steady, obedient life of one who keeps short accounts with God, his work faithfully done, his heart set on Christ, prepared each day to meet his God. Blessed is that servant whom his Lord, when He cometh, shall find watching; be ye also ready, for the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not.
